title: MB7-06983
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Venezuela who has appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

Mr. XXXX XXXX was an employee of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX) since 2007. He fears persecution on the basis of his political opinion by the government of Venezuela, the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service and armed paramilitary groups (collectivos). Mr. XXXX XXXX alleged that he suffered harassment and attacks by personnel of XXXX and by collectivos that support the government of Venezuela. He alleges that his employer perceived him to be an opponent of the governing regime as a result of his refusal to attend marches in support of the socialist party and the governing regime in Venezuela. He alleges that, in XXXX 2016, he was unfairly blamed for damage to a XXXX XXXX that caused monetary losses to the XXXX by delaying a shipment. Mr. XXXX XXXX came to Canada in XXXX 2016 and, while he was in Canada, the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service delivered a subpoena to his home requiring him to be questioned about the damage to the XXXX XXXX. Mr. XXXX XXXX decided to claim asylum in Canada when individuals from an armed group showed up at his home in Venezuela to threaten his family and assault his spouse in XXXX 2016. Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse, mother and children ended up joining him in Canada and claimed asylum at the border in XXXX 2016. This appeal only concerns Mr. XXXX XXXX' asylum claim.

The RPD accepted Mr. XXXX XXXX' allegation that he had problems at work. However, it did not find credible his allegations in relation to the prospective risk he would face if he were to return to Venezuela. The RPD also did not find the testimony of Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse and mother to be credible regarding the alleged incident in XXXX 2016 in which collectivos attended at their home to threaten and assault them. Mr. XXXX XXXX argues that the RPD erred in making its credibility findings and in not taking into account relevant evidence in the NDP for Venezuela regarding the prospective risk he would face if he were to return to Venezuela.

With the greatest of respect for the RPD member in this case, I grant the appeal. The determinative issue is whether there exists a serious possibility that Mr. XXXX XXXX would face persecution on the basis of his political opinion if he were to return to Venezuela. I do not agree with many of the reasons why the RPD questioned Mr. XXXX XXXX' credibility as well as the credibility of his spouse and mother. Ultimately, I find that, when the testimonial and documentary evidence is considered in conjunction with the evidence in the most recent NDP for Venezuela, there is sufficient credible evidence to establish that Mr. XXXX XXXX would face a serious possibility of persecution based on his political opinion if he were to return to Venezuela today. This is particularly the case due to the more detailed evidence in the most recent NDP for Venezuela on the treatment of government employees who are suspected of being traitors and also the evidence regarding incidents where the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service has mistreated persons who are perceived to be opponents to the governing regime.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.1 The exception to this rule is that the RAD may apply a deferential standard in some circumstances.2 I have conducted my own independent assessment of all of the evidence in this case, including the audio-recording of the hearing. Unless specifically stated and explained below, I have applied a correctness standard in this case. ANALYSIS Errors in the RPD's credibility analysis Error regarding omission of XXXX XXXX, 2012 incident
Mr. XXXX XXXX argues that the RPD erred in finding that he had failed to mention in his BoC an incident that occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2012 to which he testified at the hearing.

In its decision, the RPD found that Mr. XXXX XXXX had omitted to mention an incident on XXXX XXXX, 2012 in which he refused to take part in a march in support of the governing regime and his supervisor told him that he would suffer the consequences of his refusal. However, upon reading Mr. XXXX XXXX' BoC, it can be seen that he did in fact mention the XXXX XXXX, 2012 incident with his supervisor.3 In his BoC, Mr. XXXX XXXX stated that, on XXXX XXXX, 2012, several colleagues told him that he had to go to an event in support of President Hugo Chavez. He stated in his BoC that, quickly after that, he went to his supervisor's office to tell him he was unable to attend the march and that he would not waste his time supporting ideals he did not share. He then stated that his supervisor told him that he would have to "abide by the consequences". In his BoC alleged that, since this time, his work situation became uncomfortable as it was clear that he did not support the governing Chavist regime.

Based on the above, I find that the RPD erred in finding that Mr. XXXX XXXX omitted mention of the XXXX XXXX, 2012 incident in his BoC. Therefore, it also erred in concluding that the credibility of his account of events was undermined by the omission. Reasonable explanation for failure to search for another job
Mr. XXXX XXXX argues that the RPD erred in finding that his credibility was severely undermined by his failure to search for other employment after his problems at work started.

The RPD found that Mr. XXXX XXXX' failure to search for another job demonstrated an absence of fear of persecution. In my view, Mr. XXXX XXXX' explanation for why he had not searched for other employment was reasonable. Mr. XXXX XXXX testified that he had not searched for other employment because "it is not easy to get a job nowadays in Venezuela".4 He testified that he decided to "follow the current" at work until the incident where he was blamed for the damage to the XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2016.

On some level, I can understand why the RPD might be skeptical about Mr. XXXX XXXX' failure to look for other work given that, as noted by the RPD, he had a university degree and many years of experience in his field, and he testified that many of his colleagues had quit. However, in my view, the reasonableness of Mr. XXXX XXXX' explanation for why he did not search for work must be considered in light of his own circumstances and also against the backdrop of the evidence contained in the NDP for Venezuela. Mr. XXXX XXXX had testified that had been focused on his family and on providing for his wife and three children. In addition, in my view, it is relevant that the deep economic crisis in which Venezuela finds itself today had already begun in 2015 and 2016. In this context, I do not find it unreasonable that Mr. XXXX XXXX would, at least initially, attempt to keep a low profile in his current employment rather than seek new employment. For this reason, I do not find, as the RPD did, that Mr. XXXX XXXX' failure to seek alternate employment severely undermined the credibility of his allegations. This is especially the case, for his allegations of targeting by his employer following the XXXX XXXX incident in XXXX 2016 following which he left the country within days. Error in finding lack of credibility regarding XXXX 2016 incident with collectivos

Mr. XXXX XXXX argues that the RPD erred in finding that his wife and mother lacked credibility in relation to their evidence that collectivos attended at Mr. XXXX XXXX' home to threaten the family in XXXX 2016.

The RPD found that the credibility of Mr. XXXX XXXX' mother was undermined by her failure to mention in the narrative included in her BoC that the collectivos smashed her car window when they attended at Mr. XXXX XXXX' home in XXXX 2016. The RPD found that this omission undermined not only the credibility of her allegation that the window was smashed but the credibility of her allegation that the collectivos attended at the home at all.

In my view, the RPD member erred in failing to sufficiently take into account the fact that Mr. XXXX XXXX' mother had included with her BoC a copy of Mr. XXXX XXXX' narrative which did mention the smashing of the car window. The mention of the smashing of the car window is also included in the narrative attached to the BoC filed by Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse. In addition, the RPD did not take into account the fact that the claimants had filed copies of photographs of the smashed window. In light of this other evidence, I find that it was an error to place significant emphasis on the omission of the smashed window from the narrative filed by Mr. XXXX XXXX' mother to the point of finding that it undermined the credibility of her allegations that the incident occurred at all.

In addition, I find that the inconsistencies relied upon by the RPD to find Mr. XXXX XXXX' wife not credible were not sufficiently important or central to the claim to undermine her credibility altogether. It is true that Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse did not specifically state in her BoC that the collectivos said that they had come on behalf of the government, as she alleged at the hearing. However, she did state in her BoC that the collectivos asked for her husband and said that it would be better if he appeared (in response to the subpoena) because, if he did not, the family would be murdered. In light of this, I do not agree with the importance that the RPD placed on whether or not the collectivos specifically said that they were there on behalf of the government as it was clear from her BoC narrative that this was the purpose of their attendance at the family home in XXXX 2016.

Likewise, I do not agree with the emphasis placed by the RPD on the fact that Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse testified that she initially did not think there was anything out of the ordinary when she arrived home to find five collectivos members on motorcycles in front of her house. When the RPD asked Mr. XXXX XXXX' spouse about this, she responded that it is not unusual to see people on motorbikes in Venezuela and that, while she initially did not think anything was out of the ordinary, she soon realized something was wrong as they immediately surrounded her car. While on some level, I can see why the RPD may have found it difficult to believe that Mr. XXXX XXXX' wife did not find it out of the ordinary to arrive and see the collectivos in front of their home. This initial impression is not implausible nor, in my view, is it sufficient to undermine her credibility as to the incident having occurred. Overall assessment of credibility

For the reasons set out above, I do not agree with the reasons that the RPD gave for finding that Mr. XXXX XXXX, and his wife and mother, all lacked credibility. I note that the RPD did not address in its decision the documentary evidence in this case which supported the claimants' account of events. This evidence included two letters from a lawyer that Mr. XXXX XXXX' wife consulted after the incidents in XXXX and XXXX 2016, statements from Mr. XXXX XXXX' father and sister-in-law and photos of a broken windshield. In my view, this documentary evidence must be accorded weight in support of Mr. XXXX XXXX' account of events.

I note that there were portions of Mr. XXXX XXXX' evidence that did cause me concern. He testified that, a few days after he was blamed for the XXXX XXXX incident in XXXX 2016, he came to Canada "on vacation". I do not find it credible that Mr. XXXX XXXX would leave within days of the incident, without his wife and children for a vacation in Canada. Likewise, Mr. XXXX XXXX initially testified that he did not know anyone else in Canada who had worked for XXXX and later testified that one his former colleagues had come to Canada and filed a successful asylum claim. While I find that this evidence raised concerns about Mr. XXXX XXXX' willingness to be forthright in his testimony, I find that these concerns and the concerns with which I agreed above are insufficient to displace the presumption of credibility in this case. Error in assessment of prospective risk
I agree with Mr. XXXX XXXX that the RPD erred in assessing his prospective risk of persecution if he were to return to Venezuela.

While the RPD raised concerns with Mr. XXXX XXXXs' credibility, it did not question the credibility of his allegation that his employer questioned him regarding the damage to the XXXX XXXX. It also did not question the credibility of the subpoena that the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service delivered to Mr. XXXX XXXX wife in XXXX 2016, a copy of which was entered into evidence. Instead, the RPD found that this evidence was insufficient to find that Mr. XXXX XXXX would face a serious possibility of persecution based on his political opinion if he returned to Venezuela.

It must be remembered that the standard of proof in this case is not a balance of probabilities but the lower standard of a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground. Although on some level I understand why the RPD took the view that the situation alleged by Mr. XXXX XXXX amounted to little more than an accusation of workplace negligence. However, in my view, the escalation of the matter up to the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service takes on a different hue when one takes into account what I have found are his presumed truthful allegations of being seen as an opponent of the governing regime and the attendance of collectivos at his home in XXXX 2016.

This is especially the case when one takes into account the evidence in the current NDP for Venezuela about the mistreatment by the government and pro-government groups of former government employees who are viewed as opposing the governing regime.5 The NDP for Venezuela also indicates that, in 2016, the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service detained dozens of people on allegations of planning, fomenting, or participating in violent anti-government actions, including some that were in fact peaceful protests. In several cases, prosecutors failed to present any credible evidence linking the accused to crimes.6 This government crackdown on perceived political opponents has only intensified in recent years.7 While there is no evidence to suggest that Mr. XXXX XXXX was a political activist, he was a public employee who was viewed as not being supportive of the government and there is a serious possibility that he was viewed as someone who had engaged in sabotage against the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

In light of my finding that there was insufficient reason to displace the presumption of credibility in this case and also in light of the evidence in the NDP for Venezuela referred to above, I find that the evidence is sufficient to establish that Mr. XXXX XXXX would face a serious possibility of persecution based on his political opinion if he were to return to Venezuela today.

For these reasons, the appeal is allowed. Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a Convention refugee.
